summary: This RFC revises how the Resource Public Key Infrastructure handles Certificate Revocation List Number extensions. It updates RFC 6487.

eli5.summary: A list of cancelled IDs has a counter. This changes how that counter is treated in the system that protects Internet routes.

questions: what is the rpki crl number extension
do rpki relying parties ignore crl number
what does rfc 9829 change in rfc 6487
subtitle: In the RPKI, validators must ignore CRL Number values and rely on the CRL named in the issuer's current manifest.

tldr.problem: X.509 CRLs carry a CRL Number so relying parties can tell which CRL is newest, but in the RPKI exactly one CRL is already identified by the issuer's manifest, so processing the number only adds complexity and fragility.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates RFC 6487 so that RPKI relying parties MUST ignore the CRL Number extension, apart from basic format checks, and find the relevant CRL through the issuer's current manifest and the certificate's CRL Distribution Points.
tldr.outcome: CAs still include the extension, and are RECOMMENDED to set it equal to the manifest number. The manifest's hash gives a cryptographic guarantee of the intended CRL and removes possible replay vectors.

facts.label: CRL extensions per RPKI CRL
facts.value: Exactly two: AKI and CRL Number

today: RFC 9829 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025. It updates RFC 6487 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why CRL Numbers Are Redundant in the RPKI
sections.content:
A Certificate Revocation List (CRL) carries a CRL Number extension, a monotonically increasing sequence number defined in RFC 5280. It lets a relying party (RP) decide which of several usable CRLs supersedes another.

In the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) that choice never arises. A well-formed manifest fileList contains exactly one entry for its CRL, with a collision-resistant digest of the contents. The CRL Distribution Points extension of a resource certificate points at the same CRL listed on the issuing CA's current manifest. So an RP can always identify exactly one current CRL for each CA, and the ordering job of the CRL Number is covered by the monotonically increasing manifest number (RFC 9286).

The extension is still mandatory in RPKI CRLs, for compliance with the X.509 v2 CRL profile. The RFC says any use of it by RPs only adds complexity and fragility to certification path validation, so it mandates that RPs ignore it. It updates RFC 6487.
sections.eli5: If there is already a trusted sign saying 'this is the current list', counting page numbers on the lists is extra work that can go wrong. So checkers skip it.

sections.title: One Relevant CRL per Certificate
sections.content:
The RFC clarifies that for a given resource certificate there is exactly one CRL that is appropriate for checking revocation. It is the unique CRL object that is both the target of the certificate's CRL Distribution Points extension and listed in the issuing CA's current manifest fileList with a matching hash.

One consequence is stated directly: a resource certificate cannot be validated without consulting the current manifest of the certificate's issuer.
sections.eli5: To check a pass, you look at the list the office names as current, and only that one. You cannot skip asking the office.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 6487 Section 5
sections.content:
Two passages of RFC 6487 Section 5 are replaced.

First, the old rule that the CRL with the highest CRL Number supersedes all other CRLs from the same CA is gone. The new text says CAs issue new CRLs with a monotonically increasing number as in RFC 5280, and it is RECOMMENDED that the CRL Number match the manifestNumber of the manifest that will include the CRL.

Second, the old text said an RPKI CA MUST include the Authority Key Identifier and CRL Number extensions and that RPs MUST be prepared to process them. The new text says a CA MUST include exactly two extensions in every CRL, the AKI and the CRL Number, and no others are allowed. RPs MUST process the AKI extension. RPs MUST ignore the CRL Number extension except for checking that it is marked non-critical and holds a non-negative integer less than or equal to 2^159-1.
sections.eli5: CAs still number their lists, and are encouraged to use the same number as the office's folder number. Checkers only make sure the number looks sane, then ignore it.

sections.title: Changes to Path Validation
sections.content:
Step 5 of the resource certification path validation in Section 7.2 of RFC 6487 is also adjusted. The check that the issuer has not revoked the certificate still means finding the certificate's serial number on the issuer's current CRL. That CRL is now identified by the issuer's current manifest and the certificate's CRLDP, rather than by the CRLDP alone.

The CRL must itself be valid, and the public key that verifies its signature must be the same key that verifies the certificate.

The RFC also lists the integration of Errata 3205 among its changes from RFC 6487.
sections.eli5: When checking if a pass was cancelled, you now use the list the office names, not just any list you can find.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds no operational considerations beyond those in Section 9 of RFC 6487.
sections.eli5: Day-to-day running of the system does not change, apart from the new rule about ignoring the counter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3779, RFC 5280 and RFC 6487 apply to resource certificates and CRLs. This document makes explicit that, in the RPKI, the CRL on the issuer's current manifest is the relevant one for revocation status.

The hash in the manifest's fileList gives a cryptographic guarantee of the CA's intent that this is the most recent CRL, and it removes possible replay vectors. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The office's seal on the current list proves which list is the newest, so nobody can slip in an old list and pretend it is current.
